context: procurement- & hot-commissioning-led · separation, compression & treatment trains

brief.intro: A gas processing plant takes raw wellhead gas and, through a chain of separation, compression, dehydration and treatment equipment, turns it into a saleable, on-spec product. The programme is dominated not by buildings — there mostly aren't any — but by heavy rotating equipment (compressors, pumps) and the process piping that connects vessels, and by a long, careful pre-commissioning and start-up sequence that must happen in the right order before hydrocarbon is ever introduced. Long-lead equipment ordering starts almost on day one, because compressors and major vessels can take the better part of a year to arrive; the pipe-rack and equipment foundations exist mainly to receive them. The back end of the schedule belongs to the commissioning team: purge and dry-out, pressure testing, and a staged, safety-gated introduction of gas that cannot be rushed.

glossary.plain: construction is physically finished and checked, system by system, ready for pre-commissioning.
getting a system clean, dry and tested — ready to receive process fluid — before hydrocarbon is introduced.
pressure-testing piping with water to prove it holds pressure safely.
removing air and moisture from a system with nitrogen before introducing gas.
the safety instrumented system and emergency shutdown logic that protects the plant automatically.
proving an instrument signal travels correctly from the field to the control system.
the staged, safety-gated introduction of process gas that marks plant start-up.
pre-built equipment modules (e.g. dehydration units) delivered largely complete to reduce site work.

must_get_right: Order the long-lead rotating equipment and major vessels immediately — their delivery drives the whole programme, and the site work exists largely to receive them on time.
Commissioning is system/subsystem-based, not area-based — mechanical completion, loop checks and pre-commissioning follow process-system boundaries, not the construction sequence.
Protect the pre-commissioning and start-up window — purge/dry-out, leak testing and SIS/ESD proving cannot be compressed, and rework here costs disproportionate time.
Firewater and gas detection are safety-critical gating systems, not general MEP — they must be proven before hydrocarbon introduction, not treated as a follow-on trade.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and structural steel run a 6-day week; piping and rotating-equipment installation move to two shifts at peak to protect the mechanical-completion date; pre-commissioning and start-up run a 7-day calendar with dedicated commissioning crews per system.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs long-lead equipment procurement → foundations & pipe racks → equipment set → piping tie-in & hydrotest → rotating-equipment run-in → SIS/ESD proving → purge/dry-out → staged introduction of gas → performance test. Civil and structural steel are not on the critical path once foundations and pipe racks are ready to receive equipment.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Process design (P&IDs, equipment data sheets) is frozen before procurement; the client's utility tie-ins (power, instrument air, N2) are available for pre-commissioning; a single mobilisation; no free-issue equipment substitutions after order. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy lifts (compressors, vessels) require crane windows, clear laydown and, often, a temporary heavy-haul road; hazardous-area works require permit-controlled access; skilled commissioning resources (rotating-equipment specialists, SIS/ESD engineers) are shared across systems and are a resource constraint late in the programme.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: long-lead equipment slippage, rework from a failed hydrotest or SIS/ESD proving, and re-test loops before first gas. Schedule contingency is held immediately before purge/dry-out and before first gas rather than spread thinly across construction activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
